bookmarkMetadata.title: Carnelian
bookmarkMetadata.description: Carnelian, a red-orange chalcedony, was one of the most distinctive luxury materials of the Indus civilisation and was produced in large quantities by specialised lapidaries in Gujarat. Major sources in Kutch, Saurashtra, and the Rajpipla region supplied raw nodules that Harappan craftsmen fashioned into long barrel beads and “etched” or bleached designs, hallmark features of Harappan bead technology. Carnelian travelled widely across West Asia, appearing in Mesopotamian centres such as Kish, Ur, Nippur, Eshnunna, and Assur. Mesopotamian records list carnelian as a valued import from Meluhha and Dilmun, indicating its long-standing commercial significance. The stone circulated along maritime routes connecting Gujarat–Makran–Dilmun and via overland corridors across the Iranian plateau. Harappan merchants maintained trading enclaves in Mesopotamia where both finished beads and raw nodules were exchanged, and some carnelian beads were later inscribed by Sumerian craftsmen. Carnelian was used for jewellery, ritual offerings, and elite objects, revealing Harappan integration into extensive interregional exchange.

bookmarkMetadata.title: Agate
bookmarkMetadata.description: Agate, another important chalcedony, was sourced from river gravels in Kutch, Saurashtra, and southern Gujarat and formed a core component of the Harappan bead industry. Workshops at Lothal, Gola Dhoro, and Chanhudaro produced banded and heat-treated agate beads using advanced drilling and polishing techniques. Agate beads circulated widely within the subcontinent, appearing across urban and rural settlements of the Indus realm. They also reached the Iranian plateau and Central Asia, with examples documented at Tepe Hissar, Shah Tepe, and Susa, often alongside carnelian in mixed assemblages that reflect interconnected trade systems. Earlier overland routes through Baluchistan and Helmand carried agate beads beyond South Asia, while later maritime routes connected Gujarat with Dilmun and Mesopotamia. The stone’s durability and distinctive banding made it ideal for personal ornamentation, ritual objects, and status displays. Agate bead manufacture exemplifies the standardisation, specialisation, and export-oriented scale of Harappan craft industries.

bookmarkMetadata.title: Shell
bookmarkMetadata.description: Shell was a major marine resource for the Harappans, used to make bangles, ladles, decorative inlays, and ritual items. Coastal communities along the Makran and Gujarat littoral collected large gastropods—particularly Turbinella pyrum—and processed them before sending them inland. specialised workshops at Nageshwar, Lothal, Bagasra, and Gola Dhoro show extensive evidence of cutting, sawing, drilling, and finishing, indicating a highly organised shell-working industry. Shell products travelled through well-developed trade corridors to major inland centres such as Mohenjo-daro and Harappa, where the abundance of finished shell artifacts points to coordinated distribution systems. Some varieties—such as spiny murex—were likely sourced from Oman, suggesting active Harappan engagement with maritime networks connecting Magan and Dilmun. Shell items were used for ornamentation, ritual deposition, and utilitarian tools, and the industry highlights the Harappans’ mastery of coastal resource management and their participation in trans-Arabian Sea trade.

bookmarkMetadata.title: Bitumen
bookmarkMetadata.description: Bitumen played critical roles in waterproofing, construction, and seafaring across the ancient world. In the Indus region, bitumen from deposits near Sibi in the Kachi plain and Mianwali was used extensively, most notably in the waterproof brickwork of the Great Bath at Mohenjo-daro. Its use at Mehrgarh for basket waterproofing reflects long familiarity with the material. Bitumen was central to maritime technology in the Gulf. Excavations at Ra’s al-Junayz in Oman have revealed imported Mesopotamian bitumen blocks from the Euphrates source at Hit, brought specifically for ship caulking. This bitumen was mixed with tallow, gypsum, and plant fibres to seal reed or wooden boats used in Gulf navigation. Impressions of woven mats and barnacles preserved on reused slabs indicate regular maintenance of seafaring craft. Bitumen thus moved along maritime corridors linking Mesopotamia, Oman, and the Indus, highlighting the Harappans’ deep integration into Gulf maritime exchange.

bookmarkMetadata.title: lapis Lazuli
bookmarkMetadata.description: Lapis lazuli, one of the most valued stones of the Bronze Age, was sourced primarily from the Sar-i Sang mines of Badakshan and possibly from the Chagai Hills. Although the Harappans used lapis sparingly themselves, they became major intermediaries in its trade. Early access flowed through Baluchistan and the Indo-Iranian borderlands, but by the Mature Harappan period, Shortugai—an Indus trading settlement in northern Afghanistan—provided direct control over lapis distribution. From Shortugai, Harappan merchants funneled lapis toward Mesopotamia, where it adorned elite regalia and ritual objects, including those from the Royal Cemetery of Ur. Shifts in political alignments after 2000 BCE reduced lapis availability in some Harappan regions, but its earlier circulation demonstrates the civilisation’s extensive participation in long-distance exchange systems across the Iranian plateau and West Asia.

bookmarkMetadata.title: Cotton
bookmarkMetadata.description: Cotton was among the most important agricultural products of the Indus Valley, with the Harappans recognized as early cultivators and textile producers. Archaeological impressions and textile remains indicate a mature industry involving spinning, weaving, and possibly dyeing. While references to cotton trade are brief, cotton cloth is considered a likely Harappan export, particularly to Oman and other Gulf regions where Harappan ceramics, beads, and tools appear in contexts that imply associated perishable goods. Cotton textiles likely travelled via Gujarat’s maritime routes to Makran, Dilmun, and Magan on vessels caulked with imported Mesopotamian bitumen. Within the Indus world, cotton served everyday domestic needs, but in external trade it may have been exchanged for copper and other resources. Cotton thus reflects agricultural specialization, organised textile craft production, and Harappan participation in long-distance maritime commerce.

bookmarkMetadata.title: Gold and Silver
bookmarkMetadata.description: Gold and silver functioned as prestige metals in the Indus civilisation, used largely for ornaments, ritual items, and elite objects. Gold was available in small quantities from riverine deposits in the upper Indus and Jhelum regions and from the Alech Hills of Saurashtra. Additional gold may have reached the Harappans through exchange with regions such as Karnataka, known for electrum-rich deposits. Silver was rarer, with probable sources in Rajasthan, the Panjshir Valley, and trading intermediaries along the Iranian plateau. Harappans likely accessed silver through overland routes linked to Shortugai or via interactions with Dilmun and Mesopotamia. Silver beads, bangles, and vessels occur mainly at Mohenjo-daro and Harappa, emphasizing their elite association. Both metals moved along the same exchange routes that circulated copper, stones, and crafted goods, underscoring their symbolic and economic value within Harappan society.
